title: Diagnostic Procedures
contentStatus: Built per Content Principles (60% pass, terminology + notes). This module's topics were corrected per CDD gap analysis - the original DiFacto source material had Module 5 topics duplicated from Module 3; content here is written fresh, around the corrected topic area: diagnostic tool interface, fault code tree, root cause methodology, escalation decision. Diagnostic tool interface specifics pending SME confirmation.

sections.title: From Operator Awareness to Technician Diagnosis
learningObjectives: Understand the shift in diagnostic responsibility from L2 to L3A
Recognize this module's role in the Technician track
sections.content: L2 operators are trained to recognize an issue and escalate it, not diagnose it. As a Technician, that boundary moves - you're now the person issues get escalated to. This module covers the diagnostic tool interface, how fault information is structured, and the methodology for moving from a symptom to a root cause.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's Human-Machine Interface (HMI) platform, used for fleet monitoring, mission control, and programming.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Tool Interface
learningObjectives: Understand the general purpose of the diagnostic interface, distinct from the operator-level ANT dashboard
Know what kind of information the diagnostic view exposes
sections.content: Where the operator-level ANT dashboard (covered in L1-M3) shows status and mission information, the diagnostic interface exposes deeper system state - sensor readings, subsystem health, and fault history - intended for technician-level troubleshooting rather than daily operation. The exact layout and navigation of this interface will be confirmed against DiFacto's technician documentation and added here once verified.

keyTerms.note: A technician-level view exposing deeper system state (sensor readings, subsystem health, fault history) beyond what the operator-level dashboard shows.

sections.title: Reading a Fault Code Tree
learningObjectives: Understand the general structure of a fault code hierarchy
Know how to navigate from a general fault category to a specific cause
sections.content: Fault codes are typically organized hierarchically - a broad category (navigation, power, communication, mechanical) narrowing down to a specific code identifying the precise issue. Working a fault code tree means starting broad and narrowing systematically, rather than guessing at a specific cause before confirming the general category. The specific fault code reference for MoRo will be confirmed with DiFacto engineering and added to this module once available.

keyTerms.note: A hierarchical structure organizing fault codes from broad category down to specific identified cause.

sections.title: Root Cause Methodology
learningObjectives: Understand the difference between a symptom and a root cause
Apply a structured approach to isolating root cause
sections.content: A symptom (MoRo stops repeatedly in one area) and a root cause (a specific sensor degrading, a map inconsistency, a mechanical issue) aren't the same thing - treating the symptom without identifying the cause means the issue recurs. Structured root cause work means ruling out categories systematically: confirm the symptom is reproducible, isolate which subsystem is implicated, then narrow within that subsystem using the fault code tree and diagnostic interface together.

keyTerms.note: The underlying issue producing an observed symptom, as distinct from the symptom itself.

sections.title: Documenting a Diagnosis
learningObjectives: Understand why diagnostic documentation matters beyond the immediate fix
Know what information a complete diagnostic record includes
sections.content: A diagnosis isn't complete until it's documented - the symptom observed, the diagnostic steps taken, the root cause identified, and the resolution applied. This record matters beyond the individual repair: it builds a pattern history that helps identify recurring issues across units, and it's what makes escalation to DiFacto's engineering team (when needed) efficient rather than starting from scratch.

sections.title: The Escalation Decision
learningObjectives: Know the criteria for escalating beyond technician-level repair
Understand that escalation is a normal part of the diagnostic process, not a failure
sections.content: Not every diagnosis resolves at the technician level. Escalation to DiFacto engineering is appropriate when a fault code indicates a hardware issue beyond field-serviceable scope, when a root cause can't be confidently isolated after structured diagnosis, or when a pattern suggests a design or manufacturing issue rather than a unit-specific fault. Escalating appropriately, with complete documentation, is a sign of good diagnostic judgment, not a gap in skill.

questions.question: How does the diagnostic interface differ from the operator-level ANT dashboard?
options: It exposes deeper system state (sensor readings, subsystem health, fault history) for technician-level work
It only shows the time and date
questions.feedback: Correct. The diagnostic interface is a technician-level view, distinct from the operator-level dashboard.

questions.question: How should a fault code tree generally be navigated?
options: Start with the broad category and narrow systematically to the specific cause
Guess at a specific code first, then check the category
questions.feedback: Correct. Fault code trees are navigated from broad category to specific cause, not the reverse.

questions.question: What is the difference between a symptom and a root cause?
options: A symptom is the observed effect; a root cause is the underlying issue producing it
A root cause only applies to software issues
questions.feedback: Correct. Treating a symptom without finding the root cause means the issue tends to recur.

questions.question: Why does diagnostic documentation matter beyond the immediate repair?
options: It's only required for warranty claims
It doesn't matter once the issue is fixed
It builds pattern history and makes future escalation more efficient
questions.feedback: Correct. Documentation supports pattern recognition across units and efficient escalation.

questions.question: Is escalating a diagnosis to DiFacto engineering a sign of inadequate technician skill?
options: No - appropriate escalation with complete documentation reflects good diagnostic judgment
Yes, a skilled technician should never need to escalate
Only if it happens more than once
questions.feedback: Correct. Escalation is a normal, appropriate part of the diagnostic process in the right circumstances.
